TAVI (Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation) can indeed be performed safely without balloon predilatation and with similar early results as those achieved through traditional balloon predilation. However, this approach may require fewer pacing periods, which can benefit patients in the long run.

The current evidence suggests that TAVI can be successfully performed without balloon predilation for patients with asymptomatic aortic stenosis at least 75 years old. In fact, surgical procedures to prevent paravalvular leak (PVL) and to remove any damaged parts of the valve are often unnecessary in this patient subgroup.

Additionally, studies have shown that progression of valvar aortic stenosis can be adequately predicted by the present aortic valve opening area and the degree of valvar calcification for clinical purposes. This means that patients with asymptomatic aortic stenosis at least 75 years old can typically proceed to TAVI without further intervention.

However, it's essential to note that extended aortic replacement in acute type A dissection is still considered justifiable, particularly when the entire dissected aorta and aortic arch are involved. This approach requires a complex surgical technique but offers promising early and midterm results.

Regarding MRI protocols for detecting bone metastases, the current evidence suggests that an initial whole-body MRI protocol can safely limit to only T1w imaging at 3 Tesla, with no need for additional STIR sequences. These initial results will have significant implications for department workflows, reducing examination time and potentially saving financial resources.

In conclusion, while some sub-questions require more explicit coverage, the overall answer is that TAVI can be performed safely without balloon predilatation in patients at least 75 years old with asymptomatic aortic stenosis.
